title: KV pageback pressure characterization diary
content:
Purpose and narrative:

This doc is a running diary of experiments and observations about a very specific production symptom: occasional tail latency spikes (~P99.9) that correlate with increased host<->GPU page traffic and elevated eviction rates in the model KV cache. The goal is to (1) characterize the pressure mode (what triggers pagebacks), (2) quantify how much memory bandwidth and CPU interrupt cost the pagebacks add, and (3) propose mitigations that are low-risk for near-term rollout.

Background/context (short):
- Serving runtime uses per-worker KV caches to keep past key/value activations for fast autoregressive decoding. Cache entries live on GPU HBM and when memory is tight we evict to host pinned memory or compressed spill files on local NVMe.
- Customers with mixed-sequence workloads (short chat + occasional long-document summarization) cause bursty growth of active KV working sets, producing transient cache pressure and pagebacks.
- We have fallback policies (L1->L2 to host) and async prefetch, but the interaction with OS page reclaim and PCIe memory copies looks like it's producing stalls that show up as tail latency.

High-level hypothesis:
- Tail events are dominated by synchronous pagebacks (GPU read/write to host) that are triggered by aggressive LRU eviction and by simultaneous large allocations during warmup. Pagebacks saturate interconnect and contend with active kernels, causing kernel stalls and higher latency for other requests.
- Secondary hypothesis: NUMA placement and host-side memcpy threads are occasionally throttled by kernel scheduling, amplifying tail effects on multi-tenant nodes.

Instrumentation we added (quick list):
- perf counters on host for pci bus and memcpy throughput (custom eBPF hooks).
- nvprof / Nsight traces for a few sampled tail events.
- Added counters to runtime: eviction_count, pageback_bytes, pageback_ops, pageback_latency_hist (microsecond buckets), in_flight_pagebacks, kv_lookup_hit/miss by sequence_length bin (0-64,65-256,256+).
- Flamegraphs for worker thread vs. async spill threads collected with py-spy.

Representative experiment matrix (what we ran):
- Workloads: 1) mixed chat (95% <64 tokens, 5% bursts to 2048) 2) long-batch decoding 512x128 sequences 3) adversarial long-only (all sequences 2048)
- HW: 2xA100 per node (shared by 4 workers), node has 2 CPU sockets (NUMA).
- Policies tested: LRU immediate-evict to host, LRU-defer (batch eviction windows), segmented LFU, proactive prefetch on request route, 2-tier (HBM->pinned host->NVMe).

Key findings (summarized):
- Reuse rate vs sequence mix: Mixed-chat workload shows median reuse ~72% for short-turn requests but reuse for long bursts drops to ~18% (new activations). Because long bursts allocate many unique KV segments we see eviction churn.
- Pageback throughput: During tail windows we observed sustained host<->device traffic peaks of ~420 GB/s (aggregate across two GPUs) for ~200-600ms windows. These windows line up with spikes in pageback_ops and in_flight_pagebacks.
- Bandwidth saturation consequences: When host<->GPU bandwidth exceeds ~60% of measured sustainable window (empirical threshold), active decode kernels accumulate waiting time; nvprof shows kernel stalls waiting on memcpy for ~12–30ms per token batch in the worst cases.
- CPU cost: On the host we see memcpy worker threads consuming up to 35% of a core for sustained periods during big pagebacks; interrupt / scheduling latencies on secondary socket increased tail syscall latencies. This supports the NUMA contention hypothesis.
- Eviction policy impact: Delaying eviction (batching evictions into short windows) reduced measured pageback_ops by ~23% and lowered tail latency by ~15% on mixed workloads. Segmented LFU without careful warmup made reuse for short sequences slightly worse.
- Prefetch tradeoffs: Proactive prefetching of the next expected KV pages reduced stalls for long continuous decodes but increased background bandwidth and hurt small-request P50. Prefetch needs to be route-aware.

Detailed notes and traces (selected):
- 2025-01-16: Mixed-chat experiment. At 10:42:12 UTC a P99.9 spike to 1.9s occurred. nvprof sample shows a memcpy (host->device) of 48MB started just before decode kernel; kernel queued but waited for DMA, then executed with lower SM occupancy. pageback_latency_hist bucket 50–75ms jumped.
- 2025-01-20: Stress test with adversarial long-only workload produced steady-state eviction rate of ~2.2 evictions/sec per worker and pageback throughput ~380 GB/s. Latency stable under load but recovery from sustained pressure saw a long tail if additional long requests arrived during recovery.
- 2025-01-24: Turned off async prefetch; pageback peaks became sharper but shorter; P99 improved in short workloads, worsened for continuous long runs.
- 2025-01-29: NUMA-affinity experiment: binding memcpy threads to same socket as GPU PCIe root complex reduced observed tail latency by ~9% (less cross-socket memory hops).

Open questions / puzzlers:
- Why do some pagebacks show much higher latency than others for same byte size? Possibilities: PCIe packet coalescing, kernel-level reclaim interference, or transient OS scheduler noise. Need deeper capture with perf trace around pageback syscall time.
- Is NVMe spillback being considered by kernel page reclaim heuristics? We saw cases where host memory pressure pushed pages to swap/NVMe even though we expect pinned host staging. Need to audit our host allocation flags.
- Are there interactions with CUDA unified addressing page faults that cause synchronous page migrations? Some traces suggest CUDA driver falls back to migration behavior for some allocation classes.

Immediate mitigation options (ranking by risk):
1) Eviction batching (low risk): group evictions into short windows and schedule pagebacks when interconnect use is low. Reduced pageback_ops without big hit to reuse in our tests.
2) NUMA-aware memcpy thread placement (low risk): pin spill + prefetch threads to socket local to GPU. Cheap to implement and tested positive.
3) Route-aware prefetch (medium risk): only prefetch when a request route historically demonstrates long continuation; needs routing heuristics and can be gated behind config.
4) Throttle large allocations at admission (medium-high risk): reject or queue very large sequences briefly to avoid concurrent growth events across workers. Impacts tail of user-visible latency but adds admission control complexity.
5) Move to double-buffered async transfers with QoS scheduling (higher risk): build transfer scheduler to limit aggregate bandwidth per node. More infra work but would give deterministic tail bounds.

Longer-term ideas:
- Design a node-level transfer scheduler that maintains a budgeted DMA bandwidth per tenant/worker and exposes a soft-priority queue so that small interactive requests get priority over batch prefetch/spill.
- Explore compression of spilled KV pages for host resident tier to reduce transfer bytes (evaluate CPU cost of decompress vs PCIe time saved).
- Investigate using peer-to-peer GPU copies (GPU->GPU) for model sharding scenarios to avoid host involvement.

Action items (owners + ETA):
- Asha: implement eviction-batching prototype in runtime (feature-flagged) — branch created INF-evict-batch; target A/B run 2025-02-07.
- Evan: schedule memcpy/prefetch threads pinning change + small benchmark (2025-01-31) — done, results in this doc.
- Marco: instrument perf-trace wrapping around pageback syscall and collect 20 tail events for Jan 30–Feb 2 (2025-02-04).
- Liu: experiment with compressed spill format (zstd) on a small cluster to measure CPU vs bandwidth tradeoff (2025-02-14).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working diary; expect fragmentation and raw recordings. If you saw similar tail events in your customer clusters (especially mixed-short + occasional long runs), please paste example trace IDs here.
- Priority for next week: land eviction-batching behind a flag and run the benchmark harness (mixed-chat) at 4x scale to validate the 15% tail improvement in a larger environment.

References / links:
- JIRA INF-3247 (investigation epic)
- PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/681 (eviction-batching prototype upcoming)
- Slack thread: #serving-runtime "pageback pressure" (2025-01-07 onward)

End of diary entry.

Unresolved thought: should we try a fast-path that avoids host staging for small KV pages (<=4KB) and keep them resident in a compact HBM slab? Might be low-cost and improve short-request P99.
